title: When the Visitor Falls
premise: Folklorist Theo Marchetti returns to Hollowmere to record its dying songs, only to hear the church bell that was melted down in 1911 ringing across the fields. The bell is a summons: something beneath the village has woken, and it remembers the theft of 1974, when the villagers took a child from the old well-house and passed it off as their own. Theo, who was that child's sworn companion and silent witness, must return what was taken — the truth, spoken aloud in the village's own forbidden song — before the harvest moon rises and the thing below comes up to collect. In doing so, Theo loses the family they built on silence but gains a truer one among those willing to sing with them.
about_author: Lior Thornbury is the pen name of a former archivist of regional folk music who spent a decade transcribing songs no community would perform twice. They write horror about the debts small places carry and the families people build inside them.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't Cast
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Arriving in Hollowmere, Theo records an old woman's lullaby she immediately begs him to delete, then hears the melted bell toll at dusk while every villager pretends not to. The emotional beat is dread braided with longing — Theo realizes the village still feels like home, which makes its silence feel like betrayal.

chapters.title: What We Passed Off as Ours
chapters.summary: Alternating Theo and Edith Hale's POV. Digging into parish records, Theo uncovers the 1974 theft: a child taken from the well-house, renamed, raised as the Hales' own. Edith, dying and unafraid, confesses her part. The beat is guilt surfacing — belonging built on a stolen foundation begins to crack.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, climax. On the night of the harvest moon, the ground opens along the old processional path and the taken child — grown strange, neither dead nor alive — stands at Theo's door asking to be sung home. Theo defies the village elders, who would rather feed it another silence, and begins the forbidden song in the ruined churchyard as the bell tolls wildly above.

chapters.title: The Second Verse
chapters.summary: Theo and ensemble POV, resolution. The song requires more than one voice; Edith's grandchildren, then half the village, join against their fear, returning what was taken by finally naming it. The child goes down singing, the bell falls quiet, and Theo — exiled from his old silence — stays in Hollowmere as its new keeper of songs, belonging at last to a family that tells the truth.
